extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, and typesetters preparing text in or containing languages that use the Latin alphabet
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for copyediting, typesetting, and proofreading materials in (or containing quotations in) languages that use the Latin alphabet, covering punctuation, capitalization, word division, special characters, and language-specific typographic conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify special characters by Unicode name and number
rubrics_metrics.description: Use table 11.1 to correctly identify the character by name and Unicode number (e.g., “D with stroke [U+0110]” or “d with stroke [U+0111]”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When working from an author’s hard copy, marginal clarifications may be needed for handwritten accents or special characters; always indicate the character by name and Unicode number to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) — use Unicode and current IPA
rubrics_metrics.description: Phonetic symbols using IPA notation are based on the Latin alphabet and are defined for Unicode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the latest IPA alphabet, consult the International Phonetic Association website; for more on phonetic notation consult Pullum and Ladusaw, Phonetic Symbol Guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: African languages — general capitalization and punctuation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Most African languages that use the Latin alphabet follow English capitalization and punctuation, with notable exceptions (e.g., Arabic-related and many click languages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize the names of African languages in the traditional way (e.g., Kiswahili rather than KiSwahili); be aware of language-specific exceptions such as Xhosa (isiXhosa/Isixhosa) and Ge‘ez-using languages (Amharic).

rubrics_metrics.name: African languages — special characters (Hausa, Swahili, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some African languages require diacritics and special characters not used in English; Swahili uses no additional letters or diacritics, while languages such as Hausa require specific characters (e.g., B with hook, D with hook, K with hook, Y with hook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Nigeria the y with hook may be represented with an apostrophe (’Y’y); many other diacritics are too numerous to list here—consult table 11.1 and language-specific references.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — capitalization of generic and modifying words in names/addresses
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic words denoting roadways, squares, and the like are lowercased; only the proper name (or modifying word) is capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: le boulevard Saint-Germain; la place de l’Opéra; in most geographical names the generic is lowercased and the modifying word capitalized (la mer Rouge).

rubrics_metrics.name: French — capitalization of names of buildings and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of buildings are usually capitalized; in names of organizations and institutions, only the first substantive and any preceding modifier are capitalized, but not the preceding article (except at sentence start).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: l’Hôtel des Invalides; la Légion d’honneur; la Haute-Loire; use consistent house style and consult authoritative French sources where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — hyphenated names and saints
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated names both elements are capitalized; names of religious groups are usually lowercased; in names of saints the word saint is lowercased unless part of a place-name or church name, when Saint is capitalized and hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: la Comédie-Française; un chrétien; l’Église de Saint-Pierre.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — titles of works capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Chicago recommends sentence-style capitalization for French titles (only first word, subtitle, proper nouns capitalized); an alternative (Académie practice) capitalizes the article and first substantive when title begins with a definite article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent: follow sentence-style unless a publication adopts the Académie practice; note exceptions such as the newspaper Le Monde.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — spacing and punctuation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: In French typeset material thin spaces generally occur before colons, semicolons, question marks, exclamation marks, between guillemets and enclosed text, and after em dashes introducing dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In English contexts you may follow the typographic conventions of the publication instead; if French spacing is required, apply it consistently and according to French practice (use nonbreaking spaces in electronic documents where needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: French — guillemets and quotation marking
rubrics_metrics.description: French uses guillemets (« »), often with a fixed thin space; only punctuation belonging to the quoted matter is placed within closing guillemets; opening guillemets repeat at each paragraph of a multi-paragraph quotation, closing guillemets appear only at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In English contexts guillemets may be spaced like regular quotation marks; tags such as écrit-il or dit-elle may appear within quotations without extra guillemets.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — quotations within quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: For quotations within quotations double (or sometimes single) quotation marks are used; formerly additional guillemets were employed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When guillemets are used and two quotations end simultaneously, only one set of closing guillemets appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — dialogue formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In French dialogue guillemets are often replaced by em dashes; the dash is usually followed by a thin space in French publications (not necessary in English publications); dashes are used before each successive speech and are not repeated at the end of a speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set off internal quotations within speech with guillemets if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — ellipses formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: The French often use an unspaced ellipsis of three dots attached to the preceding word (like this...) to indicate interruption; unspaced ellipses enclosed in brackets with thin spaces indicate omissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In English contexts spaced periods may be used per this manual’s recommendations; for omissions French practice uses [.. .] with thin spaces between brackets and dots.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — word-division (hyphenation) rules for vowels
rubrics_metrics.description: In French a word is divided after a vowel wherever possible; one-letter syllables at line ends or beginnings should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two or more vowels forming a single sound or diphthong are never broken; consider readability for English readers and avoid confusing breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — word-division (hyphenation) rules for consonants
rubrics_metrics.description: Division is normally made between two adjacent consonants, whether the same or different; groups of three adjacent consonants are normally divided after the first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never divide immediately after an apostrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: French — words to leave undivided and accents/ligatures
rubrics_metrics.description: French practice permits breaks after one letter and divides many short words, but in English-language publications such breaks should be avoided; words of four or fewer letters should be left undivided. Retain French accents and ligatures (including on capitals) whenever needed in English contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaining accents is helpful to readers unfamiliar with French; follow Académie recommendations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: German — reflect source spelling and orthographic changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Material quoted from German should reflect the spelling in the source; the 1998 orthography reforms (with later revisions) are widely adopted but some publications retain traditional forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult Duden for principles and details; honor author/publisher preference for older works when reprinting.

rubrics_metrics.name: German — capitalization rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In German all nouns and words used as nouns are capitalized, in ordinary sentences and in titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjectives derived from proper names are generally lowercased, with exceptions (invariable adjectives ending in -er and adjectives that are part of proper names).

rubrics_metrics.name: German — polite pronouns capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: The polite second-person pronouns Sie, Ihr, and Ihnen are capitalized; as third-person pronouns they are lowercased; familiar second-person pronouns (du, dich, dein, ihr, euch) are now lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe distinctions between polite and familiar forms and consult current usage guides for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: German — apostrophe usage
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe denotes colloquial omission of e (wie geht’s); it rarely appears before a genitive s, but is used to denote omission of s after proper names ending in an s-like sound or a silent s, x, or z (e.g., Alice’ Geburtstag, Jaspers’ Philosophie).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow contemporary German practice and consult up-to-date dictionaries for genitive conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: German — quotation marks and punctuation placement
rubrics_metrics.description: German quotations usually take reversed guillemets (» «), split-level inverted quotation marks (,,“), or, in Switzerland, regular guillemets; other punctuation is placed outside the closing quotation marks unless it belongs to the quoted matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent with the variety used by the source or house style.

rubrics_metrics.name: German — word-division (hyphenation) general rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide after a vowel wherever possible; two vowels forming a diphthong are not broken; breaks should never be made after a single vowel at the beginning or end of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to section 11.20 for lineation principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: German — consonant division and compound rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more adjacent consonants are divided before the last one unless they belong to different parts of a compound; consonant combinations ch, ck, ph, sch, and th are not divided unless they belong to separate syllables; compound words should be divided between their components whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mad-chen, Zu-cker; Meeres-ufer, Rasier-apparat.

rubrics_metrics.name: German — special characters (umlauts and eszett)
rubrics_metrics.description: German requires the eszett (ß) and three umlauted vowels (ä, ö, ü); although ae/oe/ue substitutions are seen, umlauted characters and eszett are widely available and should be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse the eszett with the Greek beta; consult post-1998 dictionaries for words where ß is replaced by ss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian — capitalization of titles and formal pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: In Italian a title preceding a proper name is normally lowercased; in commercial correspondence the formal second-person pronouns Lei and Voi and their objective forms are capitalized (Posso pregarLa...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older forms (Ella, Loro) are treated similarly; consult language-specific style manuals for nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian — quotations, dialogue, and dash conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Italian uses guillemets (« ») for quotations often without space between guillemets and text; regular quotation marks are also used. In dialogue em dashes are sometimes used; the dash is used before each successive speech and, unlike French, another dash may be used at the end of the speech if other matter follows in the same paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spaces around dashes typical in Italian texts need not be used in English contexts; punctuation like periods and commas follow the closing guillemet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian — apostrophe spacing and ellipses
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe indicates omitted letters; a space should appear after an apostrophe that follows a vowel, but no space after an apostrophe that follows a consonant. Italian uses ellipses to indicate interruptions; for omissions the dots are enclosed in brackets; Chicago recommends spaced periods in English publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: po’ duro; Voglio ... quattro milioni. For omitted material use [.. .] or similar consistent convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian — word-division (vowels and consonants) and apostrophes
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide after a vowel wherever possible and avoid one-letter syllables at line ends; certain consonant groups (ch, gh, gli, gn, qu, sc, r preceded by consonant) must never be broken; three groups of consonants may be divided; never divide immediately after an apostrophe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: acro-po-li (not a-cropoli); bab-bo; dal-l’accusa (do not split after apostrophe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italian — special characters and accents on capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Italian requires certain accented characters and although grave accents on capitalized vowels are sometimes dropped, they must be retained on stressed final syllables to avoid confusion (CANTO vs CANTO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In direct quotations retain older practice where an apostrophe replaces an accent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin — capitalization for titles of works
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient and medieval Latin works should usually be capitalized in sentence style (only first word, subtitle, proper nouns/adjectives); Renaissance and modern works or Latin works in English may be capitalized headline-style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If era is doubtful, opt for sentence style; consult section 8.158 for general capitalization rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin — word-division (syllables and consonant rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Latin word has as many syllables as vowels or diphthongs and is divided accordingly; when a single consonant occurs between vowels, divide before the consonant unless it is x; when multiple consonants come together, divide before the last consonant except for specific combinations treated as single consonants (ch, gu, ph, qu, th) and a list of consonant groups that are never broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: na-tu-ra; Cae-sar; pan-chres-tus. Compound words are divided between parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latin — special characters for vowel length
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary Latin texts often mark long vowels with a macron and short vowels occasionally with a breve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use macrons and breves as needed for pedagogical clarity; see table 11.1 for characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish — capitalization of titles and national adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: In Spanish a title preceding a proper name is normally lowercased; when abbreviated, however, titles are capitalized. Nouns and adjectives denoting nationality are lowercased, but country names are capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: el señor Jaime López but el Sr. López; los mexicanos la lengua española Inglaterra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish — inverted question and exclamation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A question or exclamation in Spanish is preceded by an inverted question mark or exclamation point and followed by a regular mark; these opening marks are integral and should be retained when Spanish is quoted in English contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ¿Qué pasa, amigo? ¡Olvídalo en ese caso!

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish — guillemets, quotation marks, and dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Spanish traditionally uses guillemets (« ») as quotation marks with punctuation inside the closing guillemets only if it belongs to quoted matter; em dashes may set off words identifying the speaker; in dialogue an em dash (or sometimes a guillemet) introduces each successive speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening dash in Spanish publications is usually preceded by a space and the closing dash followed by a space; in English contexts such spaces need not be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish — ellipses formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In Spanish publications ellipses are generally unspaced; in English contexts they may be spaced per the manual; omitted material is indicated by dots enclosed in brackets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hemos comenzado la vida juntos...; [...] El gaucho [...].

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish — word-division (vowels and diphthongs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide after a vowel whenever possible; two or more vowels forming a diphthong or triphthong may not be divided; if adjacent vowels belong to separate syllables, divide between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-ra-co-les; ba-úl, cre-er.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish — consonant division and inseparable pairs
rubrics_metrics.description: If two adjacent consonants form a combination that would not occur at the beginning of a Spanish word, break between them; consonant pairs that can occur initially (bl, br, cl, cr, dr, fl, fr, gl, gr, pl, pr, tr) are inseparable unless each belongs to a different element of a compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups of three consonants not ending with one of those pairs always have s in the middle and are divided after the s; ch and ll are now alphabetized as two-letter groups per RAE but still cannot be divided in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spanish — dividing compounds and special characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words are often but not always divided between components; Spanish employs its own set of accented and special characters that should be used where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult Real Academia Española for current orthographic rules and table 11.1 for character lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Latin-alphabet languages — follow language-specific practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Many other languages using the Latin alphabet have special considerations (Albanian unified orthography since 1972; Croatian and Bosnian use Latin; Czech uses many diacritics; Danish capitalizes polite second-person pronouns; Dutch has special IJ capitalization rules; Finnish keyboards include Swedish letters; Hawaiian uses the ‘okina; Hungarian has many accented vowels; Icelandic includes eth and thorn; Norwegian polite pronoun capitalization; Polish formal-address capitalization and syllabic division; Portuguese similar to Spanish capitalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use table 11.1 for special characters; consult language-specific references (e.g., Real Academia Española, Duden) and respect historical orthography when editing older texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hawaiian — representation of ‘okina
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘okina (glottal stop) is represented by a left single quotation mark (U+2018) and may alternatively be represented by a modifier letter turned comma (U+02BB); some authors/publishers prefer U+02BB to differentiate the glottal stop from punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware many typefaces render these glyphs identically; follow author/publisher preference and consistency (see 6.115.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish — formal-address capitalization and syllabic division
rubrics_metrics.description: In formal address the second-person plural pronoun Państwo and related forms are capitalized; division of Polish words normally follows syllabic structure (e.g., kom-pli-ka-cja); the conjunction i (and) should never appear at the end of a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe historical variants and consult contemporary Polish usage guides for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portuguese — capitalization and accented capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles and nouns/adjectives denoting nationality are capitalized as in Spanish; accented capitals, sometimes dropped in Portuguese running text, should always be used when Portuguese is presented in an English context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain accents on capital letters where they disambiguate meaning (e.g., CANTO vs CANTÓ) and use consistent typographic practice.
